title: Constructing event graph and mining critical paths of Ebola virus disease: a public health emergency analysis based on WHO disease outbreak news.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Most Ebola virus disease research focuses on clinical diagnosis or static knowledge networks, limiting dynamic spatiotemporal analysis of epidemic evolution. We examined whether an event graph derived from World Health Organization (WHO) Disease Outbreak News (DONs) could reconstruct outbreak evolution across reports and identify response-timing patterns, including delayed interventions, unactioned risk assessments, and cross-border escalation. METHODS: We retrospectively analysed 346 Ebola-related DON reports published through August 2025. We used a large language model-assisted framework to extract events and their relationships. We built an event graph in Neo4j and applied a bounded depth-first search procedure that removed cycles, generated candidate paths, and selected critical paths across six dimensions: case burden, spatial spread, international risk signals, intervention measures, path length, and graph structural importance. RESULTS: The graph comprised 2233 event nodes and 10,479 relations across 155 event groups; 47 representative critical paths were selected. Laboratory confirmation often marked the shift from uncertain signals to an organised response. Healthcare-facility exposure and community deaths served as sentinel events for infection-control review and transmission-chain investigation. Preparedness, surveillance, and contact tracing generally followed spatial spread and international-risk signals rather than general border restrictions. Repeated burden updates without documented interventions indicated potential response or reporting gaps. Although established control measures aligned with WHO advice, the report defined explicit triggers, deadlines, inter-agency handoffs, and completion indicators less clearly. CONCLUSIONS: The event graph reconstructed longitudinal outbreak and response trajectories that are difficult to capture through descriptive summaries or entity-centred knowledge graphs. Effective Ebola response depends not only on available control measures but also on activating them at appropriate transition points. This framework complements, rather than replaces, WHO guidance, real-time surveillance, and formal epidemiological causal inference.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 我们回顾性分析了截至 2025 年 8 月发布的 346 份埃博拉相关 DON 报告。
elements_zh.methods: 我们使用大型语言模型辅助框架来提取事件及其关系。我们在 Neo4j 中构建了一个事件图,并应用了有界深度优先搜索程序,该程序删除了循环,生成了候选路径,并在六个维度上选择了关键路径:案例负担、空间分布、国际风险信号、干预措施、路径长度和图结构重要性。
elements_zh.main_results: 该图包含 155 个事件组中的 2233 个事件节点和 10,479 个关系;选择了 47 条有代表性的关键路径。实验室确认通常标志着从不确定信号到有组织响应的转变。医疗机构暴露和社区死亡是感染控制审查和 传播 链调查的哨兵事件。没有记录干预措施的重复负担更新表明潜在的反应或报告差距。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 事件图重建了纵向 暴发 和响应轨迹,这些轨迹很难通过描述性摘要或以实体为中心的知识图来捕获。有效的埃博拉应对措施不仅取决于现有的控制措施,还取决于在适当的过渡点启动这些措施。该框架补充而不是取代世卫组织指导、实时 监测 和正式的流行病学因果推断。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 准备、监测 和接触者追踪通常遵循空间传播和国际风险信号,而不是一般的边境限制。尽管既定的控制措施符合世卫组织的建议,但报告对明确的触发因素、最后期限、机构间交接和完成指标的定义不太明确。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 分析的回顾性限制了验证事件图准确性的能力。事件图在指导响应行动方面的有效性没有直接评估。未评估该框架对其他疾病 暴发 的适用性。

title: Ebola Virus VP40 C-terminal Lysine Residue Mediates Lipid Interactions and Dimer-Dimer Interactions.
abstract: The Ebola virus (EBOV) matrix protein VP40 is the main driver of viral assembly and budding, processes which depend on its ability to oligomerize at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (PM). VP40 forms dimers in the cytoplasm that traffic to the membrane and assemble into higher-order oligomers, but the specific molecular determinants governing the stability of these oligomeric interfaces are not fully understood. Here, we investigate the role of the C-terminal lysine residue, Lys 326 , in mediating VP40-lipid and VP40-VP40 interactions. Using a combination of molecular dynamics simulations and computational site-saturation mutagenesis, we predicted that while Lys 326 has a minimal role in the stability of the isolated VP40 dimer, it is a critical determinant in stabilizing the interfaces of higher-order structures like tetramers and hexamers. Experimentally, mutation of this residue to alanine or aspartic acid (K326A or K326D) impaired VP40 PM localization, oligomerization, and in a charge-dependent manner, virus-like particle production. Our results indicate that a cationic residue is crucial not only for interactions with anionic phospholipids in the PM but, more importantly, for forming stabilizing networks across VP40 dimer-dimer interfaces. Together, these findings identify Lys 326 as a keystone residue that couples membrane binding to the stabilization of essential higher-order oligomers, revealing a critical interface for EBOV assembly that could be exploited for future antiviral strategies.

title: Provincial Index Case of Bundibugyo Ebolavirus Disease in South Kivu Province, Democratic Republic of Congo, 2026: A Case Report
abstract: The ongoing second-largest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) was caused by contagious Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). So far, seven provinces of the DRC including Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), Sud-Ubangi (South Ubangi), and Tshopo provinces have confirmed cases of BDBV. Here, we report the clinical characteristics of the provincial index case of BDBV 2026 infection in South Kivu, DRC, and provide information about contacts who tested positive for BDBV. Collected clinical specimens tested with Polymerase Chain Reactions confirmed BDBV in the infected index case and its connections.

title: Dialysis Toolkit for Ebola Virus Disease-Associated Acute Kidney Injury
abstract: Ebola virus disease (EVD), a high-fatality haemorrhagic fever endemic to Central and West Africa. EVD frequently presents with multiorgan dysfunction, including acute kidney injury (AKI). The management of AKI in EVD presents unique challenges owing to the infection’s highly contagious nature, the need for critical care in low-resource environments, and the logistics of providing kidney replacement therapy (KRT) in high-biohazard settings. This manuscript outlines a “dialysis toolkit” to guide clinicians managing AKI in EVD. This toolkit covers infection control protocols, preferred KRT modalities, anticoagulation strategies, effluent disposal, and machine handling. Based on existing literature and biosafety guidance, this toolkit is intended for nephrologists, intensivists, intensive care unit nurses, dialysis nurses, infection-prevention teams, and biomedical staff. With this article, we aim to balance optimal nephrological care with maximal protection for healthcare workers across both resource-rich and austere outbreak settings. Keywords: Acute kidney injury, Ebola virus disease, Dialysis, Hemodialysis, Kidney replacement therapy, Peritoneal dialysis.

title: Evolutionary dynamics of the glycoprotein (gp) gene of Zaire Ebolavirus strains and its implications across Africa
abstract: Twenty seven viral sequences were acquired from the National Center for Biotechnology Information GenBank (NCBI GenBank) and analyzed them using multiple alignments with the Fast Fourier Transform (MAFFT), and Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis (MEGA) programs. The purpose of this study was to examine the genetic variation in the glycoprotein (gp) gene among Zaire ebolavirus (ZEBOV) strains. We identified 347 mutations with a high single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) frequency at positions 2008, 2038, 2221, 2267, and 2271. Positions 2221 and 2038 showed particularly high frequencies. All four regions displayed nucleotide conservation, some parts of the gp gene are quite stable (382 - 2522), while other parts are rapidly evolving, possibly resulting in virus neutralization by antibodies. Nucleotide changes in closely related strains, Yembelengoye (AY526103.1) and Entsiami (AY526102.1), as well as Mayibout (HQ849547.1) and Mvoula (AY526104.1). This suggests that the virus population is adapting to different geographical regions. There is a need for continuous monitoring of virus evolutionary trends, expanding genomic analysis to include diverse viral genes related to replication and pathogenicity, and monitoring genetic changes globally.

title: In silico cyclic-minipeptides predicting antibody-free early-diagnosis of Ebola virus
abstract: In this work, in silico cyclic-minipeptide candidates were computationally generated aiming to develop antibody-free sandwichbased early-diagnosis of ebola virus (EBOV). Presently there are few approved early-rapid EBOV diagnosis, despite many antibody-based efforts. title: Bioinformatics-driven genomic surveillance and evolutionary tracking of emerging viral pathogens
abstract: Emerging viral pathogens pose a persistent threat to global health, making genomic surveillance and evolutionary tracking essential public health tools. This review evaluates bioinformatics tools, pipelines, and analytical approaches for genomic surveillance, pathogen tracking, and real-time evolutionary biology, assessing the strengths, limitations, and pathogen-specific applicability of each. Using a cross-pathogen, comparative framework, we examine five case studies: SARS-CoV-2, Ebola virus, monkeypox virus (MPXV), avian influenza virus, and honeybee viruses, each requiring a tailored combination of whole-genome sequencing, multiple-sequence alignment, phylogenetic tree building, and molecular clock reconstruction to reconstruct transmission chains and evolutionary dynamics. Key tools discussed include Nextstrain, GISAID, BEAST, IQ-TREE, MEGA, and Pangolin. These approaches have driven tangible public health outcomes, from mRNA vaccine development for SARS-CoV-2 to universal vaccine design efforts for avian influenza, but their impact remains constrained by uneven access to sequencing infrastructure, expertise, and computational resources. Across all five case studies, no single pipeline performs best universally: tool and platform choice must instead be matched to each pathogen’s biology and the surveillance infrastructure available in a given setting. Strengthening this capacity globally, particularly in under-resourced regions, is critical to ensuring emerging pathogens are detected and characterized in time for an effective public health response.

title: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective
abstract: Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security.

Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security.

title: Genomic analysis of early case samples from the 2025 Marburg virus outbreak in Ethiopia
abstract: In November 2025, Ethiopia reported its first outbreak of Marburg virus disease, with a case fatality rate of 64%. Here we report the analysis of seven near-complete Marburg virus genomes from seven early cases. The outbreak lineage belonged to the MARV.A.1 clade, which is closely related to genomes from historical human cases and bats. A high nucleotide identity across the seven genomes suggests human-to-human transmission after a zoonotic spillover event. These findings highlight the importance of genomic surveillance for outbreak detection, response and preparedness. Phylogenetic analysis of seven Marburg virus genomes from the 2025 outbreak in Ethiopia suggests human-to-human transmission after a spillover event.

title: Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in Ebola Preparedness and Response in South Sudan, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo: A Scoping Review
abstract: Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services are fundamental to infection prevention and control during Ebola virus disease outbreaks. However, their contribution to outbreak preparedness and response remains insufficiently synthesised, particularly in fragile and outbreak-prone settings. This scoping review examined the importance of WASH in Ebola preparedness and response in Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and South Sudan. Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Literature published between 2014 and 2026 was searched through PubMed, African Index Medicus, Google Scholar, African Journals Online (AJOL) and the World Health Organization Institutional Repository for Information Sharing (IRIS). Peer-reviewed and grey-literature sources addressing WASH, infection prevention and control, preparedness or response to Ebola in the three countries were considered. The evidence was charted and synthesised thematically. The searches displayed 1,963 results, of which 861 were captured for title, abstract, summary, or full-text screening. After eligibility assessment and cross-platform deduplication, 41 unique sources were included. Six themes emerged: WASH infrastructure and service readiness; infection prevention and control preparedness; healthcare-worker preparedness; community engagement and risk communication; cross-border surveillance and institutional coordination; and institutional, financial and logistical constraints. Reliable water supplies, sanitation facilities, handwashing stations, environmental cleaning and waste-management systems supported effective infection-control practices. Nevertheless, preparedness was weakened by inadequate infrastructure, insufficient protective supplies, limited practical training, weak maintenance systems and dependence on temporary external assistance. Evidence from Uganda documented established surveillance and rapid-response arrangements alongside persistent facility-level weaknesses, while evidence from the DRC reflected extensive outbreak experience but continuing gaps in healthcare preparedness. Evidence from South Sudan identified substantial infrastructural and humanitarian constraints. However, the uneven geographical and methodological distribution of the evidence precluded direct comparison or ranking of preparedness across the three countries. Sustainable Ebola preparedness requires WASH infrastructure, practical healthcare-worker training, community participation and cross-border coordination to be incorporated into routine health-system planning and financing. Further comparative and country-specific research is required to measure the independent contribution and long-term functionality of WASH interventions.

title: A Multi-Host Deterministic Model with Optimal Control Strategies for Marburg Virus Disease
abstract: Marburg virus disease (MVD) is a zoonotic viral haemorrhagic fever that presents continuing challenges for outbreak prevention and control. This study develops a deterministic compartmental model to examine transmission among humans, bats and monkeys, together with the contribution of environmental viral contamination. The human population is represented by susceptible, exposed, infectious, quarantined and recovered compartments, while susceptible and infected classes are considered for the animal hosts. The model incorporates direct and indirect transmission, quarantine, recovery, loss of immunity, and environmental viral shedding and decay. Non-negativity, boundedness, equilibria and reproduction-number thresholds are analysed. Latin hypercube sampling and sensitivity indices are used to examine parameter effects, while an optimal-control formulation evaluates quarantine and environmental interventions alongside behavioural responses. Under the assumed baseline parameters, model simulations indicate that environment-to-human exposure accounts for at least 99.3% of the human force of infection over the 50-day period. Environmental controls alone reduce the simulated infectious peak from 6.03 to 1.15 and the cumulative infectious burden by 85%. The combined intervention scenario produces the lowest reported objective value, although its infection trajectory is similar to that of environmental control alone. Increasing quarantine rates reduces simulated infectious peaks, whereas social distancing has limited influence in the environmentally dominated baseline scenario. These results underscore the importance of assessing multiple transmission routes when selecting interventions, while recognising that the findings depend on model structure and assumed parameter values.

title: A Synthetic Consensus Chiroptera IFN-β Induces IFN-I Signaling Across Diverse Bat Taxa
abstract: Bat-associated viruses consistently spill over from bats into humans and other animals. Many bat-associated viruses, including Marburg virus and Nipah virus, cause severe disease in humans but their presentation is subclinical in bats. Advancements in tools and resources to study bat innate antiviral immune responses, including the type I IFN (IFN-I) pathway, are needed to evaluate the mechanisms that underlie differential infection outcomes between reservoir bats and spillover hosts. Commercially available IFN-Is are not bat-specific, and conspecific IFN-Is are impractical to produce for the over 1,500 described bat species. Here, we design and validate a bat order-level consensus IFN (Chiroptera IFN-β) that is functional in bat cells from six diverse bat families, including representatives from both suborders. Using Jamaican fruit bat cells, we demonstrate that Chiroptera IFN-β induces an IFN-stimulated gene repertoire comparable to conspecific IFN-β. This valuable resource can accelerate the capacity of the field to study bat innate antiviral responses and illuminate differences between bats and humans.

title: Generation-time distortion is an emergent property of epidemic control
abstract: We find that a vast space of public health interventions necessarily reshape the intervals between successive infections, known as generation times, for directly-transmitted infectious diseases (e.g., COVID-19, Ebola virus, influenza). While some studies have connected specific interventions (e.g., contact-tracing, isolation) to shifted generation times, most epidemiological analyses assume these intervals are stationary. We reveal that this assumption is substantially more fragile than previously recognised. We develop a universal microscopic representation for all intervention mechanisms that reduce individual-level infectiousness and establish generation-time reshaping as a fundamental macroscopic feature of those interventions, emerging at the population level. By constraining the topology of our representation to reflect specific mechanisms, we explain and unify previous studies as well as predict generation-time phenomena yet to be observed. We further show that neglecting generation-time reshaping can under- or over-estimate intervention effectiveness and disease control- lability by 100%, under realistic parameter settings. A stringent intervention can even produce no estimated transmissibility difference. Generation-time distortion causes unavoidable and underrated biases that can severely limit model-driven public health policy and pandemic preparedness.

full_text: A República Democrática do Congo, na África Central, enfrenta o maior surto da espécie Bundibugyo do vírus Ebola já registrado. Até 25 de outubro, foram confirmados 10.060 casos e 4.887 mortes, segundo autoridades de saúde congolesas. De cada dois diagnósticos confirmados, um terminou em morte. Até o momento, é o segundo maior surto de Ebola em número de casos. Os casos se concentram no leste do país, perto das fronteiras com Uganda e Ruanda. Na tentativa de obter novas ferramentas para conter o avanço da doença, na sexta-feira, 23 de outubro, começaram os testes com a vacina Ervebo, do laboratório farmacêutico Merck. analysis_en.study_design_and_population: O estudo Tumaini é o primeiro ensaio clínico que avalia vacinas candidatas contra o vírus Bundibugyo. Ele começou em 23 de outubro de 2026 e envolveu quatro pessoas até 27 de outubro, todas com contato com pacientes infectados pelo vírus Ebola.
analysis_en.methods: A vacina Ervebo foi administrada a participantes que tiveram contato com pacientes infectados pelo vírus Ebola. analysis_en.main_results: Até 27 de outubro, quatro pessoas haviam tomado a vacina Ervebo, todas com histórico de contato com pacientes infectados pelo vírus Ebola. Não foram relatados resultados específicos sobre a eficácia da vacina contra a espécie Bundibugyo.

analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Essa iniciativa pode fornecer dados cruciais sobre a eficácia da vacina Ervebo contra a espécie Bundibugyo, contribuindo para a formulação de estratégias de contenção e prevenção do surto de Ebola no leste da República Democrática do Congo.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: O estudo ainda está em andamento e não possui resultados completos sobre a eficácia da vacina contra Bundibugyo. A evidência é limitada a uma pequena amostra e a ausência de dados sobre a resposta imune específica a essa espécie.

Até 25 de outubro, foram confirmados 10.060 casos e 4.887 mortes, segundo autoridades de saúde congolesas. De cada dois diagnósticos confirmados, um terminou em morte. Até o momento, é o segundo maior surto de Ebola em número de casos. Os casos se concentram no leste do país, perto das fronteiras com Uganda e Ruanda. Na tentativa de obter novas ferramentas para conter o avanço da doença, na sexta-feira, 23 de outubro, começaram os testes com a vacina Ervebo, do laboratório farmacêutico Merck. Trata-se de uma vacina licenciada para prevenir a doença causada pelo vírus Ebola da espécie Zaire e sua eficácia contra Bundibugyo ainda é desconhecida. Essa vacinação é o ponto de partida do estudo Tumaini, o primeiro ensaio clínico que avalia vacinas candidatas contra o vírus Bundibugyo. Se a Ervebo não proteger contra a espécie que está causando o surto, duas candidatas inéditas serão testadas em seguida. O primeiro participante do novo ensaio recebeu uma dose dessa vacina em Bunia. Até 27 de outubro, quatro pessoas haviam tomado a vacina. Todos tiveram contato com pacientes infectados pelo vírus Ebola. Variedades de ebola Existem seis espécies de ebolavírus. A espécie Zaire causou as epidemias da África Ocidental (2014-2016) e de Kivu (2018-2020). O imunizante Ervebo foi usado em Kivu, que registrou cerca de 3.500 casos, e foi decisivo para a contenção da epidemia. Ainda não há vacina ou tratamento específico para a variedade Bundibugyo, identificada em Uganda em 2007. Antivirais e anticorpos monoclonais candidatos estão sendo avaliados em estudos clínicos.
